subject: Asada et al. (1997)
object: Asada et al. (1997) generated mice lacking GAD67 by gene targeting. Gad67 -/- mice were born at the expected frequency but died of severe cleft palate during the first morning after birth. In the cerebral cortex of newborn Gad67 -/- mice, GAD activity was reduced to 20% and GABA content to 7%, but the brain showed no discernible defects. The authors concluded that this was the first demonstration of a role for GAD67-derived GABA in the development of nonneural tissue.

subject: Asada et al. (1997)
object: Asada et al. (1997) noted that, in contrast, their earlier GAD65 -/- mice showed no change in brain GABA content or behavior apart from a slight increase in susceptibility to seizures.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families (Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish, Iranian, Brazilian) with a syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Seizures began in the first 2 months of life in all patients, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures, and early EEG showed suppression-burst, burst attenuation or hypsarrhythmia. Eight patients had joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus, 7 had cleft palate and 2 had omphalocele. All living patients had profound psychomotor delay, and 4 died before 4 years of age.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) described 2 sibs (a boy and a girl) born to Algerian first-cousin parents (Family A). Both had cleft soft palate. The boy had developmental regression, axial hypotonia and hypsarrhythmia by 5 months of age and progressed to spastic tetraparesis with no speech at 6 years. His sister had spasms from 2 days of age with a suppression-burst EEG; seizures were controlled by 3 months with levetiracetam and vigabatrin, but she had severe developmental delay with axial hypotonia.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: In 2 affected sibs from a consanguineous Algerian family (Family A), Chatron et al. (2020) found a homozygous splice site variant in GAD1, c.1414-1G>C, by exome sequencing. The variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with the disease. cDNA analysis of parental lymphoblastoid cells showed no normal mRNA from the mutant allele and 3 aberrant isoforms: one skipping exon 15, one retaining 76 bases of intron 14, and one lacking the first 7 bases of exon 15.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) described a sister and brother born to Egyptian first-cousin parents (Family B). Both had omphalocele, talipes equinovarus and arthrogryposis and developed epileptic spasms and eye twitches at 2 weeks of age. Both became seizure-free on vigabatrin. The girl also had cleft soft palate, jejunal atresia, multiple dysmorphic features, hypoplastic corpus callosum, cerebral atrophy and scoliosis. The girl died at 2 years and the boy at 4 years.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: In the affected sibs of Egyptian Family B, Chatron et al. (2020) identified a homozygous 3-bp deletion in exon 7 of GAD1, c.695_697delAGA, which deletes a highly conserved lysine (p.Lys232del; reported as p.Lys231del in the table). The variant was absent from public databases, and in silico tools predicted that it disrupts splicing. In a cell-free assay, the mutant protein was expressed at levels comparable to wild type. The authors noted that this assay bypasses splicing and could not formally demonstrate loss of function, but considered the variant pathogenic given the phenotype.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) described a sister and brother born to Turkish first-cousin parents (Family C). Both had cleft palate and refractory epilepsy that began in the neonatal period with myoclonic seizures and a suppression-burst EEG. Brain MRI was normal in both. The 12-year-old sister had profound intellectual disability, tetraparesis, talipes, conductive hearing loss and photosensitivity. The brother died of refractory seizures at 2 years of age.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: In the affected sibs of Turkish Family C, Chatron et al. (2020) used whole-genome sequencing to identify a homozygous 5-bp deletion in GAD1, c.812_816delTTAAG, which causes a frameshift (p.Val271AspfsTer9). Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variant segregated with the disease.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) described 2 sibs from an Iranian second-cousin family (Family D) with myoclonic seizures and epileptic spasms beginning in the first week of life and profound developmental delay. Neither had cleft palate, joint contractures or pes equinovarus. They also described 2 brothers from a Turkish first-cousin family (Family E). The older brother had cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, pes equinovarus, flexion contractures, facial dysmorphism and hypsarrhythmia, with epileptic spasms from 1 month of age. His brother, born at 29 weeks, had cleft palate, myoclonic seizures, congenital heart disease and pes equinovarus and died on day 9.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) identified the same homozygous nonsense variant in GAD1, c.1591C>T (p.Arg531Ter), in Persian Family D and Turkish Family E. They suggested that a common haplotype was possible given the families' relative geographic proximity.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) described a 7-year-old girl born to Brazilian first-cousin parents (Family F). Facial twitches began at 7 days of age, and EEG showed suppression-burst. Her seizures were refractory until vigabatrin was started at 11 months of age. She had profound developmental delay, choreoathetotic movements, spasticity of the lower limbs, severe scoliosis, and cerebral atrophy with ventricular dilation. She had no cleft palate and no dysmorphic facial features.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: In the Brazilian patient (Family F), Chatron et al. (2020) identified a homozygous missense variant in GAD1, c.1525G>A (p.Glu509Lys). The variant was absent from gnomAD and affects an extremely well-conserved residue in the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain. Structural modeling predicted that it disrupts salt bridges with Arg316, Lys318 and Lys389 and no longer fits into the domain core.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) found that the GAD1 variants segregated with the disease in all families in a manner consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Four of the 6 families carried truncating variants, which supports a loss-of-function mechanism. They also noted that GAD1 has a gnomAD pRec score of 0.934.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) suggested that the non-neural features (cleft palate, omphalocele, pes equinovarus and joint contractures) are secondary to reduced fetal movement caused by severe CNS involvement, as described in Gad1-null mice. They noted that biallelic loss-of-function variants in humans fully reproduce the combination of epilepsy, cleft palate and omphalocele seen in animal models.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) noted phenotypic variability between Families D and E, which carry the same variant: Family D lacked pes equinovarus, joint contractures and cleft. They suggested that genetic background or environmental factors affecting movement in utero might explain this difference.

subject: Chatron et al. (2020)
object: Chatron et al. (2020) observed a remarkably good seizure response to vigabatrin in 5 of 7 treated patients. They cautioned that the response may reflect seizure type, since epileptic spasms respond well to vigabatrin whatever the cause, and called for validation of vigabatrin as a targeted treatment.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) described a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused by biallelic GAD1 variants. It was marked by seizures starting in early infancy and by hypotonia, with variable non-CNS features such as skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features and cleft palate.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients (3 male, 3 female) from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian and Turkish ancestry; 4 of the families were consanguineous. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age. They were mainly focal motor seizures, with some patients also having epileptic spasms, focal non-motor seizures or bilateral motor seizures. Seizures were controlled with medication in 3 patients and were drug-resistant in 3. At seizure onset, EEG showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Brain MRI was normal in all but 2 patients: 1 had slight ventricular enlargement and 1 had moderate global atrophy.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) found severe developmental delay in all patients. Most never developed speech or non-verbal communication, and intellectual disability was severe in 5 patients and moderate in 1. Five of 6 patients had reduced muscle strength or tone: 4 lacked head control or could not sit or crawl, and 2 depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Mild facial dysmorphism was seen in 4 patients, and 1 had cleft palate. Other features without a common pattern included hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs, congenital hip dislocation, high myopia and hearing impairment. Metabolic workups were normal.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) noted that cognitive development did not improve even when seizures were controlled: although 3 of 6 patients became seizure-free, all had severe intellectual disability. The authors hypothesized that GAD1 variants affect development independently of seizure control.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) described one Egyptian patient (Family E, patient III-3), the child of first-cousin parents, who was the only patient born with cleft palate. She also had congenital bilateral hip dislocation with a shallow acetabulum, talipes equinovarus, hearing impairment, severe hypotonia and global brain atrophy. A similarly affected sibling died without genetic testing.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) found that the GAD1 variants segregated with disease according to autosomal recessive inheritance, confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Variants were homozygous in 5 families and compound heterozygous in 1.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.1691A>G (p.Asn564Ser) missense variant in GAD1 in a Persian girl (Family A) born to double-first-cousin parents. Her phenotype was relatively mild: moderate intellectual disability, simple speech, and seizures that became controlled. The variant was seen once in the heterozygous state in gnomAD, had a CADD score of 26.1 and was predicted pathogenic by SIFT, MutationTaster and PolyPhen-2. It lies in the C-terminal catalytic domain, and in silico analysis predicted reduced protein stability.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.971T>G (p.Phe324Cys) missense variant in GAD1 in a Pakistani boy from a consanguineous family (Family B). The variant had a gnomAD minor allele frequency of 0.00000796 (2 heterozygotes) and a CADD score of 28, and all prediction tools rated it damaging. It lies in the PLP-binding domain, and in silico analysis predicted reduced protein stability.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1040C>T (p.Thr347Met) missense variant in GAD1 in a Sudanese boy whose parents were second cousins (Family D). He had epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia, severe hypotonia and severe dysmorphic features. The variant had been reported twice in the heterozygous state in gnomAD and had a CADD score of 29.1. In silico analysis predicted that it breaks H-bonds in the PLP-binding domain. A heterozygous sister had a different neurodevelopmental condition without seizures.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.87C>G (p.Tyr29Ter) nonsense variant in GAD1 in an Egyptian patient whose parents were first cousins (Family E). The variant was absent from all queried population databases and had a CADD score of 35. The authors predicted that it causes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and complete loss of function.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.568delC (p.Gln190SerfsTer11) frameshift variant in GAD1 in a Turkish patient whose parents were first cousins (Family F); both parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was absent from gnomAD and the other population databases queried, and was classified as pathogenic under ACMG guidelines.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous GAD1 variants in an African American boy (Family C) whose parents were not reported as consanguineous: a c.1591C>T (p.Arg531Ter) nonsense variant (CADD score 43, reported only in the heterozygous state in gnomAD) and a c.670delC (p.Leu224SerfsTer5) frameshift variant. His mother carried c.670delC; his father was not available for testing.

subject: Neuray et al. (2020)
object: Neuray et al. (2020) concluded that the phenotype probably results from loss of function. They based this on four null variants, missense variants located in the PLP-binding and C-terminal catalytic domains, and the moderate intolerance of GAD1 to loss-of-function variation. They suggested that reduced GABA synthesis disrupts the balance of GABAergic signaling and so predisposes to seizures.

subject: von Hardenberg et al. (2020)
object: von Hardenberg et al. (2020) reported rational therapy with vigabatrin and a ketogenic diet in a patient with GAD1 deficiency.
